notes.definition: Phytomining and bioleaching are biological methods for extracting metals, especially copper, from low-grade ores. They avoid digging, moving and disposing of large amounts of rock, and produce metal compounds that are then processed by displacement with scrap iron or by electrolysis.
explanation: The Earth's resources of metal ores are limited. Copper ores are becoming scarce because the high-grade ores (rich in copper) have been mined first. What is left are low-grade ores, which contain only a small percentage of copper, and waste heaps from old mines. Extracting copper from these by traditional mining would mean digging up, moving and disposing of huge amounts of rock for a small amount of metal, which uses lots of energy and damages the landscape.

Phytomining uses plants to absorb metal compounds from the soil. Certain plants are grown on land containing low-grade ore or mine waste. The plants take up metal compounds through their roots and concentrate them in their tissues. The plants are then harvested and burned, and the ash produced contains metal compounds in a much higher concentration than the original soil. Phytomining is slow, as plants take time to grow, but it can also clean up land contaminated with metals.

Bioleaching uses bacteria to produce leachate solutions that contain metal compounds. Bacteria break down the low-grade ore and release metal ions into solution. The leachate (the solution produced) contains copper compounds, which can then be processed. Bioleaching is also slow, and the leachate can be toxic if it escapes into the environment, so it must be carefully contained.

The metal compounds from phytomining or bioleaching are processed to obtain the metal. For copper, the compounds are dissolved (the ash can be dissolved in acid) to make a solution of a copper compound such as copper sulfate. Copper can then be obtained by displacement using scrap iron, because iron is more reactive than copper: Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu. Alternatively, copper can be obtained by electrolysis of the solution, with copper being deposited at the negative electrode: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu.

You should be able to evaluate these biological methods. Advantages: they allow metal to be extracted from low-grade ores and waste that would otherwise be uneconomic; they avoid digging, moving and disposing of large amounts of rock; they use less energy than traditional mining and smelting; they conserve limited supplies of high-grade ore; phytomining can clean up contaminated land. Disadvantages: both are slow; phytomining needs large areas of land; bioleaching can produce toxic solutions; and the metal compounds still need further processing.
keyFacts: Metal ores are limited; high-grade copper ores are becoming scarce.
Low-grade ores contain only a small percentage of metal.
Phytomining: plants absorb metal compounds, are harvested and burned; the ash contains metal compounds.
Bioleaching: bacteria produce leachate solutions containing metal compounds.
Both methods avoid digging, moving and disposing of large amounts of rock.
Copper is obtained from its compounds by displacement with scrap iron or by electrolysis.
Displacement: Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu (iron is more reactive than copper).
Electrolysis: copper forms at the negative electrode, Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu.

keyTerms.definition: An ore containing only a small percentage of metal or metal compound.
Using plants to absorb metal compounds from the ground; the plants are harvested and burned to give ash containing metal compounds.
Using bacteria to produce leachate solutions containing metal compounds from low-grade ores.
The solution containing metal compounds produced by bioleaching.
A reaction in which a more reactive metal takes the place of a less reactive metal in its compound.
Using electricity to decompose an ionic compound in solution or when molten; metals form at the negative electrode.

workedExamples.title: Mass of copper in plant ash
workedExamples.question: Plants from a phytomining site produce 50 kg of ash. The ash contains 4.0% copper by mass. Calculate the mass of copper in the ash.
steps: Mass of copper = percentage ÷ 100 × mass of ash.

workedExamples.title: Mass of rock that must be moved
workedExamples.question: A low-grade ore contains 0.25% copper by mass. Calculate the mass of ore that must be mined to obtain 1.0 tonne of copper by traditional mining.
steps: 0.25% means 0.25 tonnes of copper in every 100 tonnes of ore.
workedExamples.answer: 400 tonnes of ore (almost all of it waste rock), which shows why traditional mining of low-grade ore is uneconomic.

workedExamples.title: Reacting mass for displacement
workedExamples.question: Scrap iron is added to copper sulfate solution from bioleaching. Calculate the mass of iron needed to produce 12.7 g of copper. Relative atomic masses: Fe = 56, Cu = 63.5.
steps: Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu: 1 mol Fe gives 1 mol Cu.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think phytomining produces pure copper directly from the plants.
misconceptions.right: In fact burning the plants gives ash containing copper compounds, which must then be processed by displacement or electrolysis.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think bioleaching uses plants.
misconceptions.right: In fact bioleaching uses bacteria; phytomining uses plants.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think these methods are used because they are fast.
misconceptions.right: In fact both are slow; they are used because they can extract metal from low-grade ores without moving huge amounts of rock.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think any metal can be used to displace copper from its solution.
misconceptions.right: In fact only a more reactive metal displaces copper; scrap iron is used because it is more reactive and cheap.

realWorld: A large share of the world's copper comes from bioleaching of low-grade ore heaps, for example in Chile.
Phytomining plants (hyperaccumulators) have been trialled to recover nickel from metal-rich soils while cleaning up contaminated land.
Scrap iron is used to recover copper from copper sulfate solutions draining from old mine sites.
higherTier: This whole subtopic is Higher tier only.
Copper ores are becoming scarce; phytomining and bioleaching extract copper from low-grade ores.
Phytomining: plants absorb metal compounds; harvested and burned; ash contains metal compounds.
Bioleaching: bacteria produce leachate solutions containing metal compounds.
Copper is obtained from solutions of its compounds by displacement using scrap iron or by electrolysis.
Evaluate biological methods: avoid digging, moving and disposing of rock; use low-grade ores; but slow.
examTips: Do not mix up the methods: phytomining = plants (phyto means plant), bioleaching = bacteria.
Always say what happens next: the metal compounds are processed by displacement with scrap iron or by electrolysis.
In evaluation questions, the key advantage to state is that they avoid digging, moving and disposing of large amounts of rock.
For displacement, explain using reactivity: iron is more reactive than copper.
Write the electrode half equation correctly: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu at the negative electrode.
summary: Copper ores are becoming scarce, so low-grade ores must be used.
Phytomining: plants absorb metal compounds; burned to ash containing metal compounds.
Bioleaching: bacteria produce leachate solutions of metal compounds.
Copper is obtained by displacement with scrap iron or by electrolysis.
Benefits: no large-scale digging, moving or disposing of rock; uses low-grade ores.

questions.question: Which method uses plants to extract metal compounds from the ground?
markScheme: 1 mark: Phytomining
questions.explanation: Phytomining uses plants. Bioleaching uses bacteria.

questions.question: What does bioleaching use to extract metal compounds?
markScheme: 1 mark: Bacteria
questions.explanation: Bacteria produce leachate solutions that contain metal compounds.

questions.question: Why are phytomining and bioleaching being developed for copper?
options: Copper is the most reactive metal
Copper cannot be extracted by electrolysis
Copper is found uncombined in the ground
markScheme: 1 mark: copper ores are becoming scarce
questions.explanation: High-grade ores are running out, so methods that use low-grade ores are needed.

questions.question: In phytomining, what is done with the plants after they have absorbed metal compounds?
options: They are left to rot in the soil
markScheme: 1 mark: harvested and burned
questions.explanation: Burning concentrates the metal compounds in the ash.

questions.question: Which metal could be used to displace copper from copper sulfate solution?
markScheme: 1 mark: Iron
questions.explanation: Only a more reactive metal displaces copper. Silver, gold and platinum are less reactive than copper.

questions.question: During electrolysis of copper sulfate solution, where is copper metal produced?
options: As a gas at both electrodes
markScheme: 1 mark: at the negative electrode (cathode)
questions.explanation: Positive Cu²⁺ ions are attracted to the negative electrode, where they gain electrons: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu.

questions.question: Which is the main advantage of bioleaching compared with traditional mining of low-grade ore?
options: It avoids digging, moving and disposing of large amounts of rock
It does not need any further processing
markScheme: 1 mark: avoids digging, moving and disposing of large amounts of rock
questions.explanation: Bioleaching is slow and produces a solution that still needs processing, but it avoids huge amounts of earth moving.

questions.question: Which ionic equation represents the displacement of copper by iron?
markScheme: 1 mark: Fe + Cu²⁺ → Fe²⁺ + Cu
questions.explanation: Iron atoms lose electrons (oxidised) to form Fe²⁺; copper ions gain electrons (reduced) to form copper. Sulfate ions are spectator ions.

questions.question: In the reaction Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu, which species is reduced?
markScheme: 1 mark: Copper(II) ions
questions.explanation: Cu²⁺ gains two electrons to become Cu, which is reduction. Iron atoms are oxidised.

questions.question: A sample of plant ash from phytomining has a mass of 200 g. It contains 6.5% copper by mass. Calculate the mass of copper in the ash.
markScheme: 1 mark: 13 g

questions.question: A low-grade copper ore contains 0.4% copper by mass. Calculate the mass of ore, in tonnes, that would need to be dug up to obtain 2 tonnes of copper.
markScheme: 1 mark: 500 tonnes
questions.explanation: 0.4% = 0.004 as a fraction. 2 ÷ 0.004 = 500 tonnes of ore, mostly waste rock.

questions.question:
Calculate the mass of copper that is produced when 2.8 g of iron reacts completely with excess copper sulfate solution.
Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu
Relative atomic masses: Fe = 56, Cu = 63.5
markScheme: 1 mark: moles Fe = 2.8 ÷ 56 = 0.05 mol
1 mark: moles Cu = 0.05 mol (1:1 ratio)
questions.explanation: The equation shows a 1:1 mole ratio, so 0.05 mol of iron gives 0.05 mol of copper.

questions.question: One hectare of phytomining plants gives 12 tonnes of dry plant material. Burning the plants leaves ash with a mass equal to 5% of the dry plant material. The ash is 8% copper by mass. Calculate the mass of copper, in kg, obtained from one hectare. (1 tonne = 1000 kg)
markScheme: 1 mark: mass of ash = 0.05 × 12 000 kg = 600 kg
1 mark: mass of copper = 0.08 × 600
1 mark: 48 kg
questions.explanation: Work in steps: plant mass to ash mass, then ash mass to copper mass.

questions.question: A bioleaching solution contains 1.6 g of copper ions per dm³. Calculate the mass of copper in 250 dm³ of the solution.
markScheme: 1 mark: 400 g
questions.explanation: Mass = concentration × volume = 1.6 × 250 = 400 g.

questions.question: Describe how phytomining is used to obtain copper compounds.
markScheme: 1 mark: plants are grown on land containing copper (low-grade ore) and absorb copper compounds
1 mark: plants are harvested and burned; the ash contains copper compounds
questions.explanation: Plants concentrate the metal compounds; burning removes the organic material to leave ash.

questions.question: State what is meant by a low-grade ore.
markScheme: 1 mark: an ore containing only a small percentage (amount) of metal
questions.explanation: Low-grade ores contain little metal compared with the mass of rock.

questions.question: Name the solution produced by bacteria in bioleaching.
markScheme: 1 mark: leachate
questions.explanation: The leachate contains metal compounds released by the bacteria.

questions.question: Explain why scrap iron can be used to obtain copper from a solution of copper sulfate.
markScheme: 1 mark: iron is more reactive than copper
1 mark: so iron displaces copper from the solution (copper metal forms)
questions.explanation: A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from its compounds.

questions.question: Give two disadvantages of phytomining.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any two: slow (plants take time to grow) / needs large areas of land / depends on growing conditions / the ash still needs further processing
questions.explanation: Plants take a long time to grow and absorb metal compounds, and only a small mass of metal is produced per area.

questions.question: Write the half equation for the reaction at the negative electrode when copper sulfate solution is electrolysed.
markScheme: 1 mark: correct species (Cu²⁺, e⁻, Cu)
1 mark: balanced with 2e⁻
questions.explanation: Each copper ion gains two electrons to form a copper atom, which is reduction.

questions.question: Old copper mine waste heaps contain about 0.1% copper. Explain why bioleaching is more suitable than traditional mining and smelting for extracting copper from these heaps.
markScheme: 1 mark: the copper content is very low, so traditional methods would need huge masses of rock to be dug, moved and processed
1 mark: this would use lots of energy and be uneconomic / produce large amounts of waste
1 mark: bioleaching extracts the copper in place without moving the rock (so it is cheaper and less damaging)
questions.explanation: Biological methods make low-grade sources economic by avoiding large-scale earth moving.

questions.question: Suggest one environmental risk of bioleaching and one way to reduce it.
markScheme: 1 mark: risk: leachate (toxic or acidic solution) may leak into soil or rivers and pollute them
1 mark: reduce: line or contain the heap / collect and treat all the solution
questions.explanation: The solutions contain dissolved metal compounds and acids that could harm living organisms.

questions.question: A mining company wants to extract copper from an area with low-grade ore. Evaluate the use of phytomining and bioleaching, compared with traditional mining, and describe how pure copper would be obtained from the products of these methods.
markScheme: Indicative content: phytomining: plants absorb copper compounds, harvested and burned, ash contains copper compounds; bioleaching: bacteria produce leachate containing copper compounds; advantages: use low-grade ores and waste, avoid digging, moving and disposing of large amounts of rock, less energy, less damage to landscape, conserve high-grade ores, phytomining can clean contaminated land; disadvantages: both slow, phytomining needs large land area, bioleaching leachate may be toxic, products need further processing; obtaining copper: dissolve ash in acid to form copper compound solution; displacement with scrap iron (iron more reactive), Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu; or electrolysis with copper deposited at negative electrode, Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu; conclusion weighing slowness against environmental and economic benefits.

Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): both methods described, a balanced evaluation with advantages and disadvantages compared with traditional mining, and correct description of obtaining copper by displacement or electrolysis, with a justified conclusion.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): both methods described with some advantages or disadvantages and some reference to processing.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements about one method.
questions.explanation: Strong answers link each advantage to low-grade ore and include the final step of processing to copper metal.

questions.question: Compare phytomining and bioleaching as methods of extracting copper.
markScheme: Indicative content: similarities: both biological, both used for low-grade ores, both avoid moving large amounts of rock, both slow, both produce copper compounds needing further processing; differences: phytomining uses plants, bioleaching uses bacteria; phytomining product is ash, bioleaching product is a leachate solution; phytomining needs harvesting and burning (releases carbon dioxide); bioleaching solution may be toxic.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): at least one similarity and at least two differences clearly stated.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): describes one or both methods without clear comparison.
questions.explanation: A comparison needs both similarities and differences, not two separate descriptions.

questions.question: What is present in the ash produced in phytomining?
markScheme: 1 mark: copper (metal) compounds
questions.explanation: The ash contains metal compounds, which must be processed to get the metal.

questions.question: State one advantage of using scrap iron, rather than new iron, to displace copper.
markScheme: 1 mark: it is cheaper / makes use of waste iron / conserves iron ore
questions.explanation: Scrap iron is a cheap waste material, so using it saves money and resources.

questions.question: A student says that 'bioleaching is better than phytomining in every way'. Which statement is the best response?
options: Correct, because bacteria are faster than any other method
Incorrect, because bioleaching cannot extract copper
Correct, because bioleaching needs no further processing
Incorrect, because each has drawbacks: bioleaching can produce toxic leachate, while phytomining can also clean up contaminated land
markScheme: 1 mark: incorrect, each method has drawbacks and benefits
questions.explanation: Evaluation needs balance: both methods are slow, both need further processing, and each has particular benefits and risks.
